title: Maps: keys and values
summary: Match each key with one value using a map. Update a locker count, look it up safely, and see why updating a key does not add another key.
introduction: A classroom chart can match each locker number with the number of books inside. A map stores pairs like these so a program can ask for the value that belongs to a chosen key.
learningObjectives: Look up a key while handling a missing key
Distinguish a map from a particular map implementation

blocks.text: A **map** holds pairs. The **key** is the label you look up. The **value** is the information stored for that label. Here locker 2 is a key and its book count is a value.
Each key has one value. Giving an existing key a new value replaces the old value. Different keys may have equal values. A **dictionary** is another common name for a map.
Map is a rule, not a promise to use hashing. C++ std::map stores a tree. Several other library maps use hashing. Our C version is a short array of pairs searched from front to back.

items: Store locker 2 with 3 books, and locker 5 with 1 book.
Update locker 2 to 6 books. Keep the same key.
Check that locker 2 exists, then print its value, 6.
Print the number of keys, 2. Updating a value did not make a third key.

blocks.text: Choose one tab. All six programs do the same task and print the same result. JavaScript can run here. The other languages need the separate local tools in [Language setup](/tutorials/data-structures-algorithms/language-setup).

blocks.text: The value for key 2 changes from 3 to 6. Key 5 still holds 1. The C++ search returns a position-like result; found->second reads the value stored at that result. Only the requested value and size print, so map order does not matter.
Check the small and tricky cases
A missing key is different from a stored value of 0. Ask whether the key exists instead of assuming that zero means missing. C# TryGetValue checks and reads in one step.

The C example updates and finds existing keys only. A reusable version would also need a way to add new pairs and grow its storage safely. Its lookup is O(n), because it scans the pairs. It is not a hash table.
C++ std::map uses O(log n) lookup in its tree. Hash-based maps aim for O(1) average lookup but can be slower when many keys collide. Learn the behavior first, then check the chosen tool's cost.

items: Change the new book count for locker 2 from 6 to 8.
The output becomes 8 then 2. The value changed again, but there are still only two keys.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: Do not use a key as though it were an array position. Key 500 can label one entry in a map with only two entries. It does not mean there are 501 entries.
